html:
Herding of cattle, sheep and goats reached East Africa about 5,000 years ago, coming south from the drying Sahara and the Nile valley. Herders spread through the grasslands of the Rift Valley long before farming took hold there.

The first herders show up around Lake Turkana in northern Kenya about 3000 BCE. There they built large cemeteries marked with stone pillars, such as Lothagam North, the oldest monuments in eastern Africa. Over the next two thousand years herding moved south into the highlands of central Kenya and northern Tanzania. Archaeologists call these later herders the Savanna Pastoral Neolithic. They made stone bowls and pottery, buried their dead in stone cairns, and probably spoke Cushitic languages.

They lived alongside hunter-gatherers, and the spread was slow, partly because cattle diseases carried by wild animals and tsetse fly blocked the way. Farming with iron tools only arrived with the Bantu expansion in the last centuries BCE. Herding went on south and finally reached the Cape about 2,000 years ago. Cattle herding is still central to peoples such as the Maasai.
sum: Herding of cattle, sheep and goats reached East Africa about 5,000 years ago, coming south from the drying Sahara and the Nile valley. Herders spread through the grasslands of the Rift Valley long before farming took hold there.
